'''Awabakal''' (also '''Awabagal''' or the '''Hunter River – Lake Macquarie''', often abbreviated '''HRLM''' language) is an [[Australian Aboriginal language]] that was spoken around [[Lake Macquarie (New South Wales)|Lake Macquarie]] and [[Newcastle, New South Wales|Newcastle]] in [[New South Wales]]. The name is derived from ''Awaba'', which was the native name of the lake. It was spoken by [[Awabakal]] and [[Wonnarua]] peoples.

It was studied by missionary [[Lancelot Threlkeld]] in the 19th century, who wrote a grammar of the language, but the spoken language had died out before 21st-century [[language revival|revival efforts]].

==Classification==

Awabakal is a [[Pama–Nyungan languages|Pama–Nyungan]] language, most closely related to the [[Worimi language]], within the [[Yuin–Kuric languages|Yuin–Kuric group]] of Pama–Nyungan.

==History==
Awabakal was studied by the Reverend [[Lancelot Threlkeld]] from 1825 until his death in 1859, producing a grammar and dictionary in ''[[An Australian Grammar]]'' in 1834.<ref name=threlkeld1834>{{Cite book | date=1834| author1=Threlkeld, Lancelot Edward | author2=White, Henry Luke | author3=Cowper, Charles | author4=Dunlop, James | author5=Ellis, William| title=An Australian grammar: comprehending the principles and natural rules of the language, as spoken by the Aborigines in the vicinity of Hunter's River, Lake Macquarie, &c. New South Wales  | publisher=Printed by Stephens and Stokes | url=https://trove.nla.gov.au/work/237350849 | access-date=23 November 2019 }} [https://nla.gov.au/nla.obj-115132947/view?partId=nla.obj-484920396 Scan1] [http://hdl.handle.net/2440/61558 Scan2]</ref> The speaker of Awabakal who taught him about the language was [[Biraban]], the tribal leader. Threlkeld and Biraban's ''Specimens of a Dialect of the Aborigines of New South Wales'' in 1827 was the earliest attempt at exhibiting the structure of an Australian language.<ref name="threlkeld">{{Cite book | publisher = C. Potter, Govt. Printer | last = Threlkeld | first = Lancelot Edward |author2=Biraban, H. Livingstone |author3=George Taplin |author4=James Günther |author5=William Grant Broughton |author6=William Ridley | url = https://archive.org/details/anaustralianlan00taplgoog | quote = An Australian language as spoken by the Awabakal, the people of Awaba, or lake Macquarie. | title = An Australian language as spoken by the Awabakal, the people of Awaba, or lake Macquarie (near Newcastle, New South Wales): being an account of their language, traditions, and customs | year = 1892 }}</ref>[[File:Dharag-Neighbors1.png|thumb|Traditional lands of Australian Aboriginal tribes of eastern New South Wales<ref>This map is indicative only.</ref>]]Threlkeld's work was greatly expanded by [[John Fraser (ethnologist)|John Fraser]] and republished in 1892 as '' An Australian language as spoken by the Awabakal, the people of Awaba or Lake Macquarie (near Newcastle, New South Wales) being an account of their language, traditions and customs / by L.E. Threlkeld; re-arranged, condensed and edited with an appendix by John Fraser''.<ref name="fraser1892">{{Cite book| date=1892  | author1=Threlkeld, Lancelot Edward | author2=Fraser, John| author3=Taplin, George | author4=Ridley, William | author5=Livingstone, H | author6=Günther, James| author7=Broughton, William Grant | via=Internet Archive  | title=An Australian language as spoken by the Awabakal, the people of Awaba or Lake Macquarie (near Newcastle, New South Wales): being an account of their language, traditions and customs | publisher=Charles Potter, Govt. Printer | url=https://archive.org/details/australianlangua00threrich/page/n12| access-date=23 November 2019|quote= Re-arranged, condensed and edited with an appendix by John Fraser }} ([https://catalogue.nla.gov.au/Record/795974 NLA catalogue entry])</ref> It contained a grammar and vocabulary as well as much new material by Fraser, and helped to popularise the name "Awabakal" for the language grouping more broadly referred to as the Hunter River-Lake Macquarie language.<ref name="threlkeld" />

== Revival ==
The language is currently being revived. A new orthography and reconstruction of the phonology has been undertaken. To date, several publications have been produced including "A grammar for the Awabakal language",<ref>{{Citation | author1=Arposio, Alex | author2=Threlkeld, L. E. (Lancelot Edward), 1788-1859 | author3=Arwarbukarl Cultural Resource Association | title=A grammar for the Awabakal language | date=2008 | publisher=Arwarbukarl Cultural Resource Association | edition= Rev. (Nov 2008) | url=https://trove.nla.gov.au/work/26604321 | access-date=26 June 2019 }}</ref> "An introduction to the Awabakal language : its orthography, recommended orthoepy and its grammar and stylistics "<ref>{{Citation | author1=Arposio, Alex | author2=Arwarbukarl Cultural Resource Association Inc | title=An introduction to the Awabakal language : its orthography, recommended orthoepy and its grammar and stylistics | date=2009 | publisher=Arwarbukarl Cultural Resource Association | edition= Rev. | isbn=978-0-9804680-5-2 }}</ref> and "Nupaleyalaan palii Awabakalkoba = Teach yourself Awabakal".<ref>{{Citation | author1=Arposio, Alex | author2=Arwarbukarl Cultural Resource Association Inc | title=Nupaleyalaan palii Awabakalkoba = Teach yourself Awabakal | date=2010 | publisher=Arwarbukarl Cultural Resource Association Inc | isbn=978-0-9804680-2-1 }}</ref>

==Grammar==

===Nouns===
There exist three [[noun class]]es. The first has 4 [[Declension|declension patterns]]. A [[noun]] can exist in any of 13 [[Grammatical case|cases]].
* 1st class – Common nouns, descriptors, [[demonstrative]]s and {{lang|awk|minaring}} {{gloss|what?}}
* 2nd class – Place names, words of [[spatial relation]]s and {{lang|awk|wonta}} {{gloss|where?}}
* 3rd class – Personal names, kinship terms, and {{lang|awk|ngaan}} {{gloss|who?}}

The default, [[Markedness|unmarked]] case of nouns is the [[Absolutive case|absolutive]]. Unlike [[English language|English]] and many [[Languages of Europe|European languages]], in which an unmarked noun is the [[nominative case]], and is (in the [[active voice]]) the [[Subject (grammar)|subject]] of the sentence, Awabakal merely references a particular noun with this case.

===Descriptors===
There is a category of words in Awabakal called descriptors. They can stand as referring terms and are in these cases similar to nouns, like [[adjectives]] or intransitive verbs/predicative verb-adjective phrases. They can be declined into nominal cases.

===Numbers===
There are four number words.
*{{lang|awk|wakool}} {{gloss|one}}
*{{lang|awk|bulowara}} {{gloss|two}}
*{{lang|awk|ngoro}} {{gloss|three}}
*{{lang|awk|wara}} {{gloss|four, five}} (also {{gloss|palm of the hand}}, a metaphorical extension of {{gloss|a handful of}})

===Pronominal enclitics===
Pronominal [[Enclitics#Classification|enclitics]] are [[suffix]]es which have several functions and can be attached to [[verb]]s, descriptors, [[apposition]]s, [[Interrogative word|interrogatives]], [[Negation (linguistics)#Grammar|negatives]] and nouns. The numbers are: [[Grammatical number|singular]], [[Dual (grammatical number)|dual]] and [[plural]] with a feminine/masculine distinction in the first [[Grammatical person|person]]. They mark verbs for person, number, case and [[Voice (grammar)|voice]]. The "[[Ergative case|ergative]]" enclitcs imply an active [[Transitive verb|transitive]] situation and the "[[Accusative case|accusative]]" implies a [[Passive voice|passive]] [[Intransitive verb|intransitive]] situation. There are three true pronouns which could be called a nominative or topic case. There are only found at the beginning of an independent clause. These pronominals are found in ergative, accusative, dative and possessive cases.

===Demonstratives===
There are 3 degrees. They are declined for 10 cases.

*'this' near the speaker
*'that' near the addressee(s)
*'that' there (but at hand)

===Appositive demonstratives===
Here too, there are 3 degrees. These terms indicate place. They decline for 13 cases.

===Verbs===
The default verbative voice of Awabakal verbs is neutral, i.e., they do not give a sense of active or passive. The pronominal enclitics indicate which voice the verb should be analysed as being in. There are 3 present tenses, 8 future and 7 past, with various voice, aspect and mood modifications.

===Negatives===
There are 10 forms of [[Negation (linguistics)|negatives]] which work with different types of words or phrases.

===Conjunctions===
[[Grammatical conjunction|Conjunctions]] are not commonly used in comparison to many languages. Sentences can often be connected without their use. These also have various combinations and case declinations.

===The Lord's Prayer===
Below is the [[Lord's Prayer]] in Awabakal, according to the Gospel of Luke.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.marysrosaries.com/Awabakal_prayers.html | title=Awabakal Rosary Prayers }}</ref> Part of the Gospel of Luke was translated into Awabakal in 1892 and below the text reflects the orthography of the prayer in 1892.

<poem>
Ġatun noa wiya barun, wiyånůn  ba,
ġiakai wiyånůn nura,
Biyuġbai ġearúmba wokka ka ba moroko ka ba kåtan, Kåmůnbilla yitirra ġiroúmba.
Ġurrabunbilla  wiyellikanne  ġiroúmba,
yanti moroko ka ba, yanti ta purrai ta ba.
Ġuwoa ġearún purreåġ ka takilliko.
Ġatun warekilla  ġearúnba yarakai umatoara, 
kulla ġéen yanti ta wareka yanti ta wiyapaiyeůn ġearúnba.
Ġatun yuti yikpra ġearún yarakai umullikan kolaġ;
mitomulla  ġearún  yarakai tabiruġ.
</poem>

==Influence on English==
The word ''[[Koori]]'', a self-referential term used by some Aboriginal people, comes from Awabakal.<ref>''[[Oxford Dictionary of English]]'', 3rd ed., p 977.</ref>
